latin.1715: XXII. Haec est Doctrina Bellarmini libri jam citati capite septimo. Ubi Respondens ad septimam objectionem affirmat, hominem in puris naturalibus conditum futurum fuisse quales nos sumus, quoad corporis mortalitatem, rebellionem membrorum, ignorantiam, difficultatem & similia. Et postea in solutione Objectionis octavae negat naturalem carnis nostrae impetum magis nunc esse rebellem, quam ante sine gratia futurus erat: & pura naturalia saniora futura fuisse ante peccatum, quam modo sint post peccatum. Adeoque in sequentibus concedit, hominem condi potuisse in tali purae naturae statu, ut in eo esset praeceps ad vitia inclinatio, & impetus sensualitatis. Et pertendit nihil absurdi sequuturum esse, si homini sic in puris naturalibus condito Deus negaret gratiam quae malis ejusmodi medetur, & homini necessaria est, ut ad beatitudinem aeternam perveniat.
latin.1716: XXIII. Caeterum negat ibidem Bellarminus, Hominem sic in puris naturalibus creatum, propterea futurum esse in diaboli potestate. Qua in re a sententia Ruardi Tapperi recedit. Is enim affirmat hominem posse a Deo creari sine Originali justitia. Et tunc non solum in eo locum habituras jam dictas infirmitates, difficultatem, & ignorantiam; sed etiam illum affligendum fore omnibus iis quae experimur malis, etiam damnatione, & daemonum vexatione. Nam, inquit, creari posset homo sine justitia Originali, & omnibus malis quae nunc experimur, affligeretur, morbis scilicet, damnatione, daemonum vexatione, & universis aliis, quae tamen in eo non essent supplicia & poenae sed cruciatus tantum, sicut sunt in bestiis. In explicatione secundi articuli facultatis Lovaniensis, pag. 72. ubi agit de peccato Originali.
latin.1717: XXIV. Quod spectat autem Protestantes, & qui inter eos speciali nomine Reformati dicuntur, communi consensu illi quoque docent Deum creavisse hominem in Justitia & Sanctitate vera: juxta illud Ecclesiastae, Deus fecit hominem rectum. Nec enim rectitudo ista alia in re consistere potest, quam in conformitate cum voluntate & lege divina, in qua hominis justitia consistit. Quo etiam Paulum respicere putant, dum fideles hortatur, ut induant novum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus est in justitia & sanctitate veritatis. Ubi manifestum est illum alludere ad primam creationem, in qua homo creatus dicitur ad Dei imaginem & similitudinem; ad quam ex ejus mente, pertinet sanctitas & justitia illa, quam Christus in fidelibus spiritu suo operatur.
latin.1718: XXV. Caeterum sanctitatem & justitiam illam in qua primus homo a Deo conditus est, non in eo solum constituunt, quod Deum creatorem suum, uti par erat, agnoscebat, & puro ac syncero amore ei adhaerebat; sed in eo quoque quod omnes ejus facultates sic bene constitutae & ordinatae erant, ut inferiores superioribus, superiores vero Deo sine difficultate & repugnantia parerent: nec in eo ulla esset aut ad malum proclivitas, aut ad bene agendum difficultas & renitentia: qualis est illa quae jam in omnibus & singulis hominibus reperitur. Proindeque ex eorum sententia, in homine recens condito nihil inordinatum, nihil immoderatum fuit. Nec in eo locum habuit ulla ἀταξία, vel pugna facultatum illius inter se: sed omnes ejus facultates summa cum εὐταξίᾳ inter se concordes atque ordinatae, eundem finem, videlicet illum ad quem a Deo naturae authore creatus fuit, conspirabant.
latin.1719: XXVI. Porro justitiam istam primo homini ante lapsum naturalem fuisse, & dici debere contendunt. Non quidem quod fuerit pars essentiam naturae humanae constituens, aut quod ex humanae naturae principiis necessario fluxerit: sed quia fuit aliquid naturae concreatum, & ad dotes nativas humanae naturae nondum lapsae pertinens. Adeoque justitia illa Originalis, secundum eorum doctrinam, donum naturale fuit, non supernaturale. Et se habet respectu animae hominis integri, quomodo respectu corporis se habebat justa membrorum proportio & pulchritudo, vigor atque decor, quae in eo tum reperiebantur, quaeque naturalem quandam, non vero supernaturalem perfectionem hominis spectabant: licet non essent de essentia hominis, neque etiam ex naturae humanae principiis necessario fluerent.
latin.1720: XXVII. Sed ut clarius & certius in hac quaestione Scholae Reformatae sententia percipiatur, operae pretium erit breviter hic referre, quomodo praecipui aliquot illius Doctores mentem suam hac de re explicent: maxime cum videri posset inter eos hic esse nonnulla diversitas. Primum igitur Tilenus Syntagmatis Theologici parte prima, Disputatione trigesima tertia, Thesi decima quarta asserit, justitiam illam recte dici naturalem, eo sensu quo naturalia & supernaturalia mutuo sibi opponuntur, & ab invicem distinguuntur. Thesi vero decima septima dicit tam naturalem primo parenti fuisse hanc justitiae originalis qualitatem, quam erat ipsa natura & forma substantialis per creationem accepta. Adeoque Thesi praecedenti affirmat qualitatem istam ex primigenia Dei in homine imagine confestim emicuisse, ut solent accidentia ex subjectis suis.
latin.1721: XXVIII. Amesius in Bellarmino Enervato tomo quarto capite primo, explicans quomodo justitia Originalis primo homini naturalis fuerit, Nos non dicimus, inquit, justitiam illam fuisse vel essentialem partem naturae Physicae, aut Physico modo ex ejus principiis fluere, sed conditionem esse moralem naturae illi debitam, quae ad juste operandum fuit creata.
latin.1722: XXIX. Josue Placeus in Syntagmate Thesium Salmuriensium Disputatione de statu Adami ante lapsum, Thesi decima octava, dicit rectitudinem originalem primi hominis naturalibus donis annumerandam fuisse, quoniam nihil aliud fuit, quam congruentia cum lege naturae, & perfectio quae fuit simul cum natura creata, & quae per naturalem generationem propaganda erat, adeoque perfectio naturalis naturalibus hominis facultatibus respondens. Thesi vero vigesima sexta concedit justitiam Originalem fuisse quidem gratiam, hoc est, donum gratuitum ab eisdem tribus personis profectum, a quibus natura ipsa creata fuit: & gratiam non fuisse, quo sensu hoc nomen opponitur naturae, & significat effecta favoris divini quo Deus peccatores prosequitur in Christo.
latin.1723: XXX. Sic vero suam ea de re mentem exponit Petrus Molinaeus. Contendimus, inquit, Adamo ante lapsum naturale fuisse Deum cognoscere & amare. Nec in natura integra agnoscimus ullam proclivitatem ad rebellionem, quia nihil erat quod coerceretur, quamvis esset quod regeretur. Nec putamus puritatem Adami ante lapsum fuisse fraenum extrinsecus injectum, aut sessorem adhibitum, sed virtutem naturalem. Disputat. de statu Innocentiae. Thesi XXV. in Thesauro Thesium Sedanensium.
latin.1724: XXXI. Pareus autem in librum Bellarmini de Gratia primi hominis cap. 1. dicit supernaturale esse quod homini supra naturae principia, vel dotes nativas inest ad ejus perfectionem. Naturam autem distinguit in integram, qualis erat in statu creationis ante lapsum, & in corruptam, qualis est in statu peccati. Unde observat supernaturale duobus modis dici. Vel enim significat id quod est supra naturam integram, vel id quod est supra naturam corruptam. Jam vero concedit justitiam originalem supernaturalem fuisse posteriori modo, quia superabat naturam corruptam. Sed negat priori modo fuisse supernaturalem, quoniam videlicet, non fuit supra dotes & perfectiones nativas naturae integrae. Capite vero quinto dicit defendi posse justitiam Originis primo homini tanquam naturae bonum fuisse naturalem, non minus quam facultatem videndi, sentiendi, &c. Quoniam ex mente illuminata notitiae illustres de Deo & rebus divinis: ex voluntate & corde justo Sancto, ut ex limpidissimo fonte operationes justae Sanctae scaturiebant, non minus naturaliter, licet mediante libero arbitrio, quam visio ex oculo, &c. Sed addit non esse necesse hoc urgere, propterea quod Adamo naturale fuit, non tantum quicquid ejus naturam constituebat, vel ex principiis naturae constitutae per se fluebat: sed etiam quicquid principiis naturae ad ejus perfectionem per se adjacebat, & sine quo natura in suis principiis non erat primitus condita. Ad quem vocis naturalis sensum potissimum spectare Theologos nostros affirmat, quum justitiam Originis primo homini fuisse naturalem contendunt. Unde colligit Bellarminum pervertere statum quaestionis, dum docet hic non quaeri, An justitia Originalis primo homini naturalis fuerit, prout naturale significat id quod inest a nativitate, quod utrinque conceditur, sed an fuerit naturalis, prout naturale distinguitur a supernaturali, & significat vel id quod naturam constituit, vel aptum est fluere ex principiis naturae.
latin.1725: XXXII. Denique Ramburtius in Sedanensium Thesium Syntagmate Disputatione de imagine Dei in homine, & justitia Originali. Thesi vigesima septima sic de hac quaestione sententiam suam pronunciat, Nos statuimus justitiam Originalem complecti totam hominis integritatem & sanctitatem, eamque homini fuisse naturalem: ita ut in Adae natura, simul atque extitit, insitum fuerit diligere Deum, eique obtemperare, hocque dono excelluisse hominem statim atque conditus est. Quod ita non volumus accipi ac si ex naturae viribus profluxerit haec sanctitas; sed quod nativa fuerit homini haec integritas: ita ut in eo per naturam, ut a Deo conditus est, & in hoc statu substitit, nulli fuerint motus inordinati: quemadmodum naturalem dicimus esse aliquam cognitionem Dei, quatenus nihil est tam naturale, quam quod ita naturae insidet, ut sine ejus, ut sic dicam, ejuratione non possit amoveri. Haec igitur justitia fulsit in Adamo simul ac exortus est, nihilque huic justitiae tepugnans expertus est.
latin.1726: XXXIII. Ex his autem apparet multos ex Reformatis manifeste docere justitiam Originalem primo homini naturalem fuisse, quoniam erat perfectio ordinis naturalis, creaturae rationali peccato nondum corruptae debita, ut quae ex naturae humanae, quae pura & innocens adhuc supponitur, facultatibus veluti emicat: non secus ac sanitas & bona valetudo ex corpore secundum naturam recte se habente. Alios vero, ut Pareum in primis, videri justitiam illam eo tantum nomine primo homini naturalem dicere, quod esset perfectio quaedam primo homini concreata, & quae ad ejus nativas & Originales dotes pertinebat. Ac quum supernaturalem illam fuisse negant, non aliud sibi velle, quam illam non fuisse aliquid primigeniis & nativis dotibus hominis superadditum.
latin.1727: XXXIV. Utcunque tamen de eo sit, & quacunque tandem ratione dicatur Originalis justitia primo homini fuisse naturalis, communis videtur esse Reformatorum sententia, omnino bonitati & sapientiae divinae repugnare, ut Deus hominem condat absque justitia Originali, & talem qui Deum, ut par est, non agnoscat & amet, & ad malum sit pronus atque proclivis, & in quo sensus atque appetitus rationi repugnant, & sint legi divinae rebelles. Nec enim existimant ejusmodi erga Deum amoris privationem, & praecipitem ad malum & vitia inclinationem, ac rebellionem sensus & appetitus adversus mentem, & legem divinam in creatura rationali posse peccato & culpa carere. Adeoque absurdum & creatori injurium ducunt, si dicatur ejusmodi inferiorum animae facultatum rebellionem, & quae inde sequitur totius hominis ad malum pronitatem, & repugnantiam ad bonum aliquid esse consequens hominis compositionem ex anima rationali & corpore organico, quodque necessario, & secundum ipsam rerum naturam inde resultat, nisi Deus aliquid supra naturam addat, quod subjiciat rationem Deo, & partem inferiorem animae rationi subdat.
latin.1728: XXXV. Ac proinde plane fictitium & impossibilem censent statum illum hominis in puris naturalibus, cujus saepe in Schola Romana mentio fit; in quo supponitur homo peccato non corruptus, & tamen justitia & sanctitate vacuus, Deoque non adhaerens puro & casto amore, sed propria concupiscentia ad inferiora tractus, ignorans quae ad veram beatitudinem necessaria sunt, ad bonum perficiendum infirmus & impotens, & ad vitia praecipiti inclinatione proclivis, sicut colligere est ex Doctorum Reformatorum, qui supra citati sunt, & plurimorum aliorum dissertationibus, dum de justitia Originali adversus Bellarminum, aliosque Doctores Scholae Romanae disputant.
latin.1729: XXXVI. Pareus tamen asserere non audet, non potuisse naturam humanam absque Originali justitia creari. Nec dicimus, inquit, naturam humanam non potuisse a Deo sine Originali justitia creari. Nos enim terminum divinae ponemus potentiae? saltem dicimus Deum, cum hominem integrum conderet, non potuisse seipsum negare; hominem integrum sine integritate condere. In libr. 1. Bellarm. de Grat. Primi hominis cap. 6. Responsione ad rationem quartam.
latin.1730: XXXVII. Porro quamvis pertendant Doctores Reformati justitiam Originalem primo homini fuisse naturalem, affirmare tamen nolunt, saltem eorum complures, primum hominem caruisse omni gratia supernaturali, & non aliis quam naturalibus donis a Deo fuisse ornatum. Illud praesertim videre est apud Petrum Molinaeum, supra citata disputatione de statu innocentiae, thesi 49. & 50. Non imus tamen inficias, inquit, quin in Adamo fuerint quaedam dona supernaturalia. Nam si aliquam cognitionem hauserat ex revelatione: aut si quid habuit ad quod humana natura quantumvis pura non potuit pervenire sine dono Dei peculiari & extraordinario, id sine dubio fuit supernaturale: nec id Adam perstans in integritate ad posteros propagasset. Praeterea quemadmodum non dubium est quin homo quantumvis perfecto corporis temperamento naturali, opus habeat auxilio supernaturali, & Dei ope continua, ad servandam hanc εὐκρασίαν: ita etsi Adami natura esset pura & sancta, opus tamen habebat jugi auxilio supernaturali ad conservandam istam puritatem. Cum etiam inanimata & irrationalia divino sustentur influxu.
latin.1731: XXXVIII. Ramburtius similiter in Adamo agnoscit dona supernaturalia, thesi vigesima nona modo citatae disputationis. Neque propterea, inquit, dona supernaturalia ab Adamo removemus. Gratia enim Dei haec eadem dona naturalia exornabat, in dies attollebat: quemadmodum gratia non destruit naturam, sed eam dirigit, & altius quam quo per vires suas eniti potest erigit. Ideo primus homo non modo fuit eximia creatura, sed etiam filius Dei, assumptus ad cernendam haereditatem caelestem, id est, non tantum habuit per naturam rationem servi fidelis, Domini voluntatem probe intelligentis, eamque perfecte exequentis, sed etiam per gratiam dignitatem filii paternam benedictionem & haereditatem sperantis.
latin.1732: XXXIX. Quibus similia apud Tilenum legere est. Criminose, inquit, & calumniose Pelagianorum sententiam nobis affingunt Pontificii, quasi nulla supernaturalia dona in primo homine fuisse contendamus, cum Theologicas virtutes ipsi tribuamus διαρρήδην. De justitia Originali thesi trigesima octava. Paulo ante vero distinctius explicans qua in re consisteret gratia Adamo collata, Ut a natura, inquit, id habebat voluntas Adami, ut posset juste & sancte operari, sic ut reapse operaretur, Deumque super omnia amaret, efficaciter movebatur a gratia. At quemadmodum vitis non propterea caret vi naturali ad proferendum vinum, quod externis illi opus est auxiliis, puta sole, pluvia & cultura, ut actu proferat, sic & in Adamo non ideo naturalis non fuit voluntatis rectitudo, & affectuum εὐταξία, licet in actu secundo gratiae moventis auxilio exercitaretur & adjuvaretur.
latin.1733: XL. Proinde Doctor ille ad gratiam supernaturalem in primo homine refert, tum auxilium actuale quo excitabatur ad bene agendum, tum virtutes Theologicas fidem, spem, & charitatem quibus ornatus erat. Sed difficile capi potest quomodo virtutes istae in Adamo fuerint dona supernaturalia, & tamen rectitudo, seu justitia Originalis ipsi naturalis erat, aut quae possit esse justitia & Rectitudo Deo grata & accepta sine fide, spe, & charitate. Ut & in iis quae ante ex Ramburtio retulimus, non satis inter se concordare videntur quae simul affirmat doctissimus ille vir, nempe primi hominis justitiam & sanctitatem naturalem fuisse non supernaturalem, & tamen eam ex viribus naturae non profluxisse. Quomodo enim potest non esse supernaturale quod ex naturae viribus non profluit? Nisi dicamus eum cum Pareo supernaturale vocare quod adventitium est, & ad nativas dotes superadditur. Originalem vero justitiam eo solum nomine naturalem vocari, quod a prima Origine fuerit homini insita, & ipsi concreata, & sic ad nativas ejus dotes pertinuerit; quomodo ipse se videtur explicare. Quanquam non satis quadrat quod subjungit, justitiam primi hominis illi fuisse naturalem, sicut naturalis nobis est aliqua Dei cognitio. Nam cognitio illa Dei quam naturalem vocat, non superat naturae vires.
latin.1734: XLI. Ex iis autem quae hactenus exposita fuerunt, planum est Scholam Romanam, & Scholam Reformatam in eo consentire, quod primus homo ante lapsum praeditus fuerit vera justitia & sanctitate, per quam & Deum mente sicuti decet agnoscebat, & voluntate diligebat, nihilque habebat in se inordinatum, & quod legi ac voluntati divinae repugnaret, quodque se ultro rectae rationi non submitteret.
latin.1735: XLII. Inde quoque manifestum est, Scholae Romanae Theologos, plerosque saltem, cum Reformatis docere primum hominem fuisse in justitia illa & sanctitate creatum; adeoque primum hominem nunquam ea caruisse, sed eam illi a prima Origine fuisse insitam.
latin.1736: XLIII. Proindeque quod illinc manifeste sequitur, plerique Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae cum Protestantibus agnoscunt justitiam Originalem primo homini naturalem fuisse, quatenus naturale significat idem quod nativum, & opponitur ei quod est adventitium & superadditum.
latin.1737: XLIV. Imo patet ex iis quae ante retulimus, in Ecclesia Romana non deesse, qui cum plerisque Reformatis doceant justitiam Originalem pertinuisse ad dona naturae, non gratiae, prout naturae opponitur: adeoque primo homini naturalem fuisse, quatenus naturale opponitur supernaturali.
latin.1738: XLV. Praeterea, ut ex dictis colligere est, in Ecclesia Romana non pauci Reformatis concedunt justitiam Originalem, qualiscunque tandem dicenda sit, seu naturalis, seu supernaturalis, fuisse perfectionem ita homini innocenti debitam, ut salva sapientia & bonitate divina, non potuerit absque illa creari: adeoque statum hominis in puris naturalibus, qualem describit Scholae Romanae vulgus, & in quo supponitur homo non peccator, & tamen justitia vacuus, & in vitia pronus, ac concupiscentia rationi rectae repugnanti laborans, esse aliquid mere fictitium; & quod bonitas, justitia, & sapientia divina in rerum natura unquam dari prohibent.
latin.1739: XLVI. Vicissim vero Protestantes Doctoribus Scholae Romanae concedunt justitiam Originalem non fuisse primo homini naturalem, quatenus naturale significat, id quod naturam constituit, aut quod necessario, sive modo physico, fluit ex humanae naturae principiis. Ac praeterea multi Scholae Reformatae Doctores non negant primum hominem habuisse dona quaedam supernaturalia: & gratiam quandam homini, etiam innocenti, necessariam fuisse, ut recte & secundum justitiam operaretur. Quin eorum nonnulli justitiam Originalem ex naturae viribus non fluxisse fatentur.
latin.1740: XLVII. Verum hic controversia est inter Scholam Romanam, paucissimis exceptis, & inter Scholam Reformatam, Num justitia Originalis primo homini naturalis fuerit, vel supernaturalis. Naturalem fuisse non supernaturalem communi consensu affirmant Scholae Reformatae Doctores; contra vero Scholae Romanae Theologi plerique omnes pertendunt illam fuisse non naturalem, sed supernaturalem. Quae quidem controversia respectu quorundam Theologorum realis, respectu vero aliorum verbalis esse videtur. Realis est respectu eorum qui sentiunt justitiam Originalem fuisse perfectionem ordinis naturalis, naturalibus hominis facultatibus respondentem, & quae non ad gratiam sed ad naturam pertinebat. Reapse enim contrarium significare volunt Scholae Romanae Theologi, quum asserunt justitiam illam fuisse supernaturalem. Sed eadem controversia verbalis est respectu aliorum, qui docent justitiam istam non aliter primo homini fuisse naturalem, quam quia erat illi concreata, & inter dotes ejus nativas numerari debet. Ac quum eandem justitiam negant fuisse supernaturalem, nihil aliud significare volunt, quam eam non fuisse homini supra primigenias dotes superadditam. Quod concedunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, saltem eorum quamplurimi.
latin.1741: XLVIII. Praeterea vero quaestio est inter Scholam Reformatam & plurimos Scholae Romanae Doctores, Annon sapientiae & bonitati divinae repugnet hominem creari absque justitia Originali; & an inter status hominis possibiles numerari debeat status ille quem Schola Romana vocat purae naturae: In quo non sit homo peccato corruptus, & tamen vera justitia careat, multaque ignorantia & infirmitate laboret, & ad malum trahatur propria concupiscentia, & appetitu adversus rationem rebellante, non secus ac res se habet in statu naturae corruptae. Quod affirmat vulgus Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae, Schola vero Reformata communi consensu negat, uno forte vel altero excepto.
latin.1742: XLIX. Et certe nisi ita statuamus, gravissima sequentur absurda. Primo enim inde sequetur concupiscentiam illam, per quam caro pugnat adversus spiritum, & quam Scholae Romanae Doctores, etiam post remissum peccatum Originale, concedunt habere rationem vitii, & mali cujusdam moralis, quod Deo displicens & odiosum est, quamque Joannes negat esse a Patre, sequetur, inquam, inde concupiscentiam illam potuisse habere Deum ipsum authorem; qui scilicet, ex hac hypothesi, hominem cum illa creare potuerit. Nec vim argumenti tollit quod Bellarminus Respondet, concupiscentiam istam ex materia fuisse emersuram, praeter Dei intentionem: Ut rubiginem ex gladio, cujus propterea faber ferrarius author non est. Nam faber ferrarius non fecit ferri materiam unde rubigo exoritur, sicut Deus corporis nostri materiam creavit. Et tamen, citra fabri culpam, non potest inesse rubigo gladio ex manibus illius prodeunti.
latin.1743: L. Posito enim quod Deus hominem aliquem creet cum eadem ignorantia, proclivitate ad malum, & repugnantia ad bonum, cum qua jam ex Adamo nascimur; nec ulla gratia supernaturali illum juvare velit, quod fieri posse censent communiter Scholastici, homo ille nec Deum diliget, nec actus & affectus suos ad normam rectae rationis componet, sed libidini suae in omnibus indulgebit, & in diversa flagitia, prout se dabit occasio necessario ruet; ut faceret homo ex Adamo natus, si omni gratiae divinae auxilio destitueretur. Ac proinde sic Deus erit author peccati; ut qui creaverit hominem, qui nulla sua culpa, sed quali illum Deo, formare visum fuit, peccatum vitare non potest, ac quodam naturae vitio & impetu in varia scelera sese praecipitem eat, nec creatorem suum, sicuti par est, diligere valet. Vel dicendum est dari posse creaturam rationalem, quae Deum agnoscere & amare non tenebitur, quaeque poterit se omni immunditia polluere, & irae luxuriae ac gulae indulgere, stuprisque & caedibus in sui similes grassari, & reliqua patrari quae lex naturae & aeterna vetat, nec tamen propterea ullius criminis & peccati rea fiet. Quorum utrumque est vehementer absurdum; & manifestam quandam impietatem involvit.
latin.1744: LI. Hoc autem semel concesso, fieri non posse ut homo a Deo creetur absque justitia & sanctitate, tanti momenti non videtur altera illa quaestio. An Justitia & Sanctitas illa in qua Deus primum hominem condidit, & sine qua creari a Deo non potuit, pertineat ad naturae, vel ad gratiae dotes, & naturalis dicenda sit, vel supernaturalis: Modo, quod omnes concedunt, statuamus illam esse gratuitum Dei donum, quod nullis creaturae meritis debebatur.
latin.1745: LII. Ratio tamen exigere videtur, ut dicamus illam ad naturae dotes pertinuisse, & naturalem potius fuisse quam supernaturalem. Etenim naturale non supernaturale est, id quod ad naturae rectam constitutionem pertinet, & sine quo natura nec sana est, nec recte constituta. Jam vero natura humana absque Sanctitate & Justitia illa, quae homini integro inerat, non sana, sed aegra est, nec potest dici recte constituta; si quidem facultatum inferiorum adversus rationem rebellio, & pronitas totius hominis ad rebellandum Deo, naturae rationalis morbus est & vitium quoddam.
latin.1746: LIII. Praeterea creaturae rationali non corruptae naturale est id sine quo naturalem suum finem assequi nequit. Sed finis creaturae rationalis est, ut Deum agnoscat, amet atque colat. Ad hoc fuit enim a Deo condita. Hunc finem autem assequi non potest, si absque justitia & sanctitate creetur; Et si consideretur ut destituta donis illis quae per Adami peccatum amisimus.
latin.1747: LIV. Nec etiam est ulla naturalis facultas cui sua perfectio naturalis non respondeat. Morales autem facultates, ratione quarum homo est virtutis & vitii capax, homini naturales sunt, non minus quam caeterae. Qua in re autem earum naturalis perfectio consistere potest, nisi in ipsa justitia & sanctitate, de qua jam quaestio est?
latin.1748: LV. Adde quod ad naturae dotes in creatura rationali non corrupta sed pura pertinet, ut conformis sit legi naturae, & ad illius regulas se componat. Ac proinde quicquid sine quo non potest naturae legi sese conformare, & omnes motus suos illi subdere, dotes & ordinem naturae non excedit. Ad legem autem naturae se componere non potest, homo destitutus omni justitia & sanctitate, & infirmitatibus illis quibuscum hodie nascimur, obnoxius. Adeoque sanctitas & justitia illa, per quam tolluntur tales infirmitates, ad naturae non corruptae dona spectare censenda est.
latin.1749: LVI. Unde videtur quoque cum ratione non satis congruere quod ex Reformatis nonnulli supra citati dicunt, licet justitia & sanctitas illa in qua primus homo creatus est, fuerit ei naturalis, illum tamen eguisse auxilio quodam supernaturali, quo ad bene agendum moveretur & excitaretur. Quanquam enim certum sit sine jugi Dei auxilio nihil boni unquam hominem agere, non tantum in rebus spiritualibus, sed ne quidem in rebus civilibus & humanis: adeoque ante lapsum ipsum opus fuisse homini perpetuo auxilio Dei, in quo vivimus, movemur, & sumus: Attamen non necesse est ut auxilium istud fuerit Ordinis supernaturalis; sed potuit ad hoc sufficere auxilium quod non superaret ordinem naturae primitus a Deo institutae. Nam auxilium requisitum ad hoc ut creatura quaeque nondum corrupta atque vitiata, naturae suae conformiter agat, & ad finem suum naturalem tendat, ad naturae ordinem pertinere existimandum est.
latin.1750: LVII. Verum inde non sequitur falsum esse quod diserte docent Reformati complures, nimirum in primo homine fuisse dona quaedam supernaturalia. Nam potuit Deus ad naturae primigeniae dotes, & auxilia ei necessaria, supra naturam quod libuit addere; sed quid illud & quantum fuerit, non audemus, scriptura tacente, definire. Illud tamen ex scriptura certum, in primo homine fuisse notitiam quandam supernaturalem: quandoquidem Deus illi supra naturam sese revelavit, & de voluntate sua expresso verbo illum edocuit.
latin.1751: LVIII. Neque ex eo quod homo constat corpore terreno & anima spirituali, sequitur in eo naturalem esse pugnam sensus & appetitus adversus rationem: adeoque talem pugnam atque rebellionem non posse tolli, nisi per donum supernaturale. Nam naturalis quidem est homini duplex inclinatio, una erga bonum terrenum, quatenus corporeus est, altera vero erga bonum spirituale, quatenus praeditus est anima intelligente: sed quemadmodum anima suo corpore longe praestantior est, ita quoque naturae recte constitutae convenit, ut corporis motus & inclinationes animae Imperiis & jussibus subjiciantur, & sic appetitus rationi pareat. Quum vero res aliter se habet, in eo apparet quaedam naturae deordinatio.
latin.1752: LIX. Nec posito quod rectitudo homini concreata ipsa naturalis fuerit, non supernaturalis, ita difficile est, ut Bellarminus existimat, ostendere qua ratione corruptio illa quae jam nobis inest, & per quam ratio cogitur affectibus subesse, naturam humanam invasit. Vitium enim illud ortum habuit a parte animi superiore, quum a Deo discedens, ferri coepit in objectum appetitus sensitivi tanquam in finem suum. Nam inde secuta est facultatum moralium in homine ἀταξία. Siquidem primigenia earum rectitudo in eo consistebat quod ad Deum tanquam finem summum omnes illarum motus & affectus, ex mentis & rationis imperio, dirigebantur. A quo fine ratio deviare non potest, & bona terrena illi substituere, quin sensui & appetitui, quorum jam objectum pro fine summo est, turpiter, & contra propriam naturam servire cogatur.

sections.title: Bellarmine: man in pure nature would be as we are, prone to vice, and could be denied healing grace
sections.pass_a: This is the Doctrine of Bellarmine in the book already cited, chapter seven. Where Responding to the seventh objection he affirms that man made in pure naturals would have been such as we are, as to mortality of body, rebellion of the members, ignorance, difficulty and similar things. And afterwards in the solution of the eighth Objection he denies that the natural impulse of our flesh is now more rebellious than it was going to be before without grace: and that pure naturals would have been healthier before sin than they are now after sin. And so in what follows he grants that man could have been made in such a state of pure nature that there would be in him a headlong inclination to vices, and impulse of sensuality. And he insists that nothing absurd would follow if God denied to man thus made in pure naturals the grace which heals evils of this kind, and is necessary for man to reach eternal blessedness.
pass_b: This is Bellarmine's teaching in chapter 7 of the book already cited. Answering the seventh objection there, he says that man created in a purely natural state would have been just as we are with respect to bodily mortality, the rebellion of the members, ignorance, difficulty and the like.

Later, answering the eighth objection, he denies that the natural drive of our flesh is more rebellious now than it would have been earlier without grace, and denies that man's purely natural endowments would have been any healthier before sin than they are now after it.

Further on he even grants that man could have been made in such a state of pure nature that he would have had a headlong bent toward vice and the drive of sensuality. And he insists that nothing absurd would follow if God refused a man so created the grace that heals these evils and that man needs to reach eternal blessedness.

choices.why: Sensualitas is the scholastic name for the lower, sense appetite; 'sensuality' keeps the technical term.

notes: Bellarmine, De gratia primi hominis, chapter 7, answers to the seventh and eighth objections.

sections.title: Bellarmine denies such a man would be in the devil's power; Tapper says he could suffer every evil, even damnation, as punishment-free torment
sections.pass_a: But Bellarmine denies in the same place that Man thus created in pure naturals would on that account be in the devil's power. In which matter he departs from the opinion of Ruard Tapper. For he affirms that man can be created by God without Original justice. And then not only would the infirmities already mentioned, difficulty, and ignorance have place in him; but also he would be afflicted with all those evils which we experience, even damnation, and vexation by demons. For, he says, man could be created without Original justice, and would be afflicted with all the evils which we now experience, namely diseases, damnation, vexation of demons, and all others, which however in him would not be punishments and penalties but only torments, as they are in beasts. In the explanation of the second article of the faculty of Louvain, page 72. where he treats of Original sin.
pass_b: In the same place, however, Bellarmine denies that a man so created in a purely natural state would for that reason be in the devil's power. Here he parts from Ruard Tapper.

Tapper holds that God can create man without original righteousness, and that such a man would then not only suffer the weaknesses already named, difficulty and ignorance, but would also be afflicted with every evil we experience, even damnation and harassment by demons.

"Man could be created without original righteousness," he says, "and be afflicted with all the evils we now experience: diseases, damnation, harassment by demons and all the rest. In him, though, they would not be punishments and penalties, only torments, as they are in the beasts." So Tapper writes in his explanation of the second article of the Louvain faculty, page 72, where he deals with original sin.

choices.why: Tapper's point is that suffering without guilt is not penal; the English keeps both penal words against 'torments'.

notes: Ruard Tapper (1487-1559), dean of the Louvain theology faculty; his commentary explains the Louvain articles of 1544.

sections.title: The Reformed agree: God made man upright, in righteousness and true holiness (Eccl. 7:29; Eph. 4:24)
sections.pass_a: But as regards the Protestants, and those among them who are called by the special name Reformed, by common consent they too teach that God created man in true Justice and Sanctity: according to that of Ecclesiastes, God made man upright. For that rectitude cannot consist in another thing than in conformity with the divine will and law, in which man's justice consists. To which also they think Paul looks, when he exhorts the faithful to put on the new man, who according to God is created in justice and sanctity of truth. Where it is manifest that he alludes to the first creation, in which man is said to be created to the image and likeness of God; to which in his mind pertains that sanctity and justice which Christ works in the faithful by his spirit.
pass_b: The Protestants, and especially those among them called the Reformed, likewise teach by common consent that God created man in true righteousness and holiness, as the Preacher says: "God made man upright." That uprightness can consist in nothing else than conformity with God's will and law, which is what man's righteousness consists in.

They think Paul has the same thing in view when he urges believers to "put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness." He is plainly alluding there to the first creation, in which man is said to have been made in God's image and likeness. In Paul's mind that image includes the holiness and righteousness that Christ works in believers by his Spirit.

choices.why: Ecclesiastes 7:29 in the familiar English wording; rectitudo then follows as 'uprightness'.

notes: Ecclesiastes 7:29 and Ephesians 4:24 are quoted without reference in the print; the image and likeness is Genesis 1:26-27.

sections.title: The Reformed: original righteousness also meant every faculty in order, with no disorder or conflict
sections.pass_a: But they place that sanctity and justice in which the first man was founded by God not only in this, that he acknowledged God his creator, as was right, and adhered to him with pure and sincere love; but also in this that all his faculties were so well constituted and ordered, that the lower obeyed the higher, and the higher God without difficulty and repugnance: nor was there in him any either proneness to evil, or difficulty and reluctance toward acting well: such as is that which is now found in each and every man. And therefore in their opinion, in man newly founded nothing was disordered, nothing immoderate. Nor did any ataxia have place in him, or fight of his faculties among themselves: but all his faculties with the greatest eutaxia agreeing and ordered among themselves conspired to the same end, namely that for which he had been created by God the author of nature.
pass_b: They do not place the holiness and righteousness in which God made the first man only in his acknowledging God as his creator, as was fitting, and clinging to him with pure and sincere love. They place it also in the good constitution and order of all his faculties: the lower obeyed the higher and the higher obeyed God without difficulty or resistance, and he had no leaning to evil and no difficulty or reluctance in doing good, such as is now found in every single human being.

So in their view nothing in newly created man was disordered and nothing was excessive. There was no disorder (ataxia) in him and no conflict among his faculties. All of them, in the most perfect good order (eutaxia), agreed with one another and worked together toward one and the same end, the end for which God, the author of nature, had created him.

choices.why: Conspirare is 'to breathe together, agree in aim'; the English avoids the modern sinister sense.

sections.title: Natural not as part of man's essence but as created with him, like the body's proportion and beauty
sections.pass_a: Further they contend that that justice was natural to the first man before the fall, and ought to be called so. Not indeed because it was a part constituting the essence of human nature, or because it flowed necessarily from the principles of human nature: but because it was something concreated with nature, and pertaining to the native endowments of human nature not yet fallen. And so that Original justice, according to their doctrine, was a natural gift, not supernatural. And it stands in respect of the soul of integral man as the just proportion and beauty of the members, vigor and comeliness, stood in respect of the body, which were then found in him, and which regarded a certain natural, not supernatural perfection of man: although they were not of the essence of man, nor also flowed necessarily from the principles of human nature.
pass_b: They further maintain that this righteousness was natural to the first man before the fall and should be called natural. They do not mean that it was a part making up the essence of human nature, or that it flowed necessarily from the principles of human nature. They mean that it was created together with that nature and belonged to the native endowments of human nature before the fall. On their teaching, then, original righteousness was a natural gift, not a supernatural one.

It stood to the soul of unfallen man as the due proportion and beauty of the limbs, their strength and grace, then stood to his body. Those belonged to a natural, not a supernatural, perfection of man, even though they were not part of his essence and did not flow necessarily from the principles of human nature.

choices.why: Concreatum is the key Reformed term: given at creation, not added later; the English spells that out.

sections.title: Survey of Reformed doctors, beginning with Tilenus: natural as opposed to supernatural, as natural as the substantial form
sections.pass_a: But so that the opinion of the Reformed School in this question may be perceived more clearly and more certainly, it will be worth the effort to report briefly here how some chief Doctors of it explain their mind on this matter: especially since it might seem that there is here some diversity among them. First therefore Tilenus in the first part of the Theological Syntagma, Disputation thirty-three, Thesis fourteen asserts that that justice is rightly called natural, in that sense in which naturals and supernaturals are mutually opposed to each other, and are distinguished from one another. But in Thesis seventeen he says that this quality of original justice was as natural to the first parent as was nature itself and the substantial form received through creation. And so in the preceding Thesis he affirms that that quality shone forth at once from the primeval image of God in man, as accidents are wont to from their subjects.
pass_b: To make the Reformed school's view on this question clearer and surer, it will be worth setting out briefly how some of its leading teachers explain their meaning, all the more because there might seem to be some difference among them here.

Tilenus comes first. In the first part of his Syntagma of Theology, disputation 33, thesis 14, he says that original righteousness is rightly called natural in the sense in which natural and supernatural are set against each other and distinguished. In thesis 17 he says that this quality of original righteousness was as natural to our first parent as nature itself and the substantial form he received in creation. And in the thesis before that he says the quality shone out at once from God's original image in man, as accidents commonly do from their subjects.

choices.why: Scholastic term for what makes a thing the kind of thing it is; kept as the technical phrase.

notes: Daniel Tilenus, Syntagma tripartitum disputationum theologicarum (Sedan).

sections.title: Ames: original righteousness a moral condition owed to a nature made to act justly
sections.pass_a: Ames in Bellarmine Enervated volume four chapter one, explaining how Original justice was natural to the first man, We do not say, he says, that that justice was either an essential part of Physical nature, or flowed in a Physical way from its principles, but that it was a moral condition owed to that nature, which was created for acting justly.
pass_b: William Ames, in volume 4, chapter 1 of his Bellarmine Disarmed, explains how original righteousness was natural to the first man: "We do not say that this righteousness was an essential part of physical nature or flowed from its principles in a physical way. We say it was a moral condition owed to that nature, which was created to act righteously."

choices.why: Ames contrasts physical (natural-causal) and moral; both words are kept.

notes: William Ames, Bellarminus enervatus (1628), volume 4, book 1, chapter 1.

sections.title: Placaeus: original rectitude a natural gift, propagated by generation; grace only as a free gift, not as Christ's favor to sinners
sections.pass_a: Josué de la Place in the Syntagma of the Saumur Theses, Disputation on the state of Adam before the fall, Thesis eighteen, says that the original rectitude of the first man was to be counted among natural gifts, since it was nothing else than congruence with the law of nature, and a perfection which was created together with nature, and which was to be propagated by natural generation, and so a natural perfection answering to the natural faculties of man. But in Thesis twenty-six he concedes that Original justice was indeed grace, that is, a gratuitous gift proceeding from the same three persons from whom nature itself was created: and that it was not grace in the sense in which this name is opposed to nature, and signifies the effects of divine favor by which God pursues sinners in Christ.
pass_b: Josué de la Place, in the Syntagma of Saumur Theses, disputation on the state of Adam before the fall, thesis 18, says that the first man's original rectitude should be counted among natural gifts. It was nothing other than agreement with the law of nature, a perfection created together with nature and meant to be handed on by natural generation, and so a natural perfection answering to man's natural faculties.

In thesis 26 he grants that original righteousness was indeed a grace, in the sense of a free gift coming from the same three persons who created nature itself. But it was not a grace in the sense in which the word is opposed to nature and means the effects of the divine favor with which God follows sinners in Christ.

lemmas.gloss: agreement with the law of nature

choices.why: The Trinity as one Creator and Giver; the English keeps Placaeus' wording.

notes: The theses are in the Syntagma thesium theologicarum in Academia Salmuriensi disputatarum.

sections.title: Du Moulin: to know and love God was natural to Adam; his purity not a bridle laid on from outside
sections.pass_a: But thus Pierre du Moulin sets out his mind on that matter. We contend, he says, that to know and love God was natural to Adam before the fall. Nor do we acknowledge in integral nature any proneness to rebellion, since there was nothing that needed to be restrained, although there was what needed to be ruled. Nor do we think that the purity of Adam before the fall was a bridle thrown on from outside, or a rider applied, but a natural virtue. Disputation on the state of Innocence. Thesis XXV. in the Thesaurus of the Sedan Theses.
pass_b: Pierre du Moulin explains his view on this as follows: "We maintain that before the fall it was natural for Adam to know and love God. In unfallen nature we recognize no leaning toward rebellion, for there was nothing that had to be held in check, though there was something that had to be governed. Nor do we think that Adam's purity before the fall was a bridle put on him from outside, or a rider set on his back, but a natural strength." (Disputation on the State of Innocence, thesis 25, in the Thesaurus of Sedan Theses.)

lemmas.gloss: had to be held in check

choices.why: Du Moulin answers Bellarmine's 'golden bridle' with the horse-and-rider image; both nouns are kept.

notes: The 'bridle' answers Bellarmine's golden bridle (thesis X of this locus).

sections.title: Pareus: supernatural above integral nature or above corrupt nature; original righteousness natural like sight; Bellarmine misstates the question
sections.pass_a: But Pareus on the book of Bellarmine on the Grace of the first man chap. 1. says that that is supernatural which is in man above the principles of nature, or native endowments, for his perfection. But he distinguishes nature into integral, such as it was in the state of creation before the fall, and into corrupt, such as it is in the state of sin. Whence he observes that supernatural is said in two ways. For it signifies either that which is above integral nature, or that which is above corrupt nature. Now he concedes that original justice was supernatural in the latter way, because it surpassed corrupt nature. But he denies that it was supernatural in the former way, since namely, it was not above the native endowments and perfections of integral nature. But in chapter five he says that it can be defended that the justice of Origin was natural to the first man as a good of nature, no less than the faculty of seeing, sensing, etc. Since from an enlightened mind illustrious knowledge about God and divine things: from a just and Holy will and heart, as from a most limpid fountain, just and Holy operations gushed forth, no less naturally, although by means of free choice, than vision from the eye, etc. But he adds that it is not necessary to press this, because to Adam was natural not only whatever constituted his nature, or flowed of itself from the principles of constituted nature: but also whatever lay adjacent of itself to the principles of nature for its perfection, and without which nature was not first founded in its principles. To which sense of the word natural he affirms our Theologians chiefly look, when they contend that the justice of Origin was natural to the first man. Whence he gathers that Bellarmine perverts the state of the question, when he teaches that it is not asked here, Whether Original justice was natural to the first man, according as natural signifies that which is in from birth, which is granted on both sides, but whether it was natural, according as natural is distinguished from supernatural, and signifies either that which constitutes nature, or is apt to flow from the principles of nature.
pass_b: Pareus, commenting on chapter 1 of Bellarmine's book On the Grace of the First Man, says that the supernatural is whatever is in man, for his perfection, above the principles of nature or his native endowments. He divides nature into unfallen nature, as it was at creation before the fall, and corrupt nature, as it is in the state of sin. So, he notes, "supernatural" is used in two ways: for what is above unfallen nature, or for what is above corrupt nature. He grants that original righteousness was supernatural in the second way, since it surpassed corrupt nature, but denies that it was supernatural in the first way, since it did not go beyond the native endowments and perfections of unfallen nature.

On chapter 5 he says it can be defended that original righteousness was natural to the first man as a good of his nature, no less than the power of seeing or sensing. For bright knowledge of God and divine things came from his enlightened mind, and righteous and holy acts welled up from his righteous and holy will and heart as from a perfectly clear spring, no less naturally, though through free choice, than sight comes from the eye.

But he adds that there is no need to press this point. What was natural to Adam was not only whatever made up his nature or flowed of itself from the principles of that nature, but also whatever of itself accompanied the principles of nature for its perfection, and without which nature was not first made in its principles. That, he says, is the sense of "natural" our theologians chiefly have in mind when they maintain that original righteousness was natural to the first man.

From this he concludes that Bellarmine twists the point at issue when he says the question here is not whether original righteousness was natural to the first man in the sense of what is there from birth, which both sides grant, but whether it was natural as natural is distinguished from supernatural, meaning either what makes up nature or what is fitted to flow from nature's principles.

choices.why: Status quaestionis is the exact question in dispute; the English names it plainly.

notes: David Pareus, commentary against Bellarmine's De gratia primi hominis, chapters 1 and 5.

sections.title: Rambour: original righteousness natural as native, not as flowing from nature's powers, like natural knowledge of God
sections.pass_a: Finally Rambour in the Syntagma of the Sedan Theses, Disputation on the image of God in man, and Original justice. In Thesis twenty-seven pronounces his opinion on this question thus, We hold that Original justice comprises the whole integrity and sanctity of man, and that it was natural to man: so that in Adam's nature, as soon as it came into being, it was implanted to love God, and obey him, and that man excelled in this gift as soon as he was founded. Which we do not want to be taken thus as if this sanctity flowed from the powers of nature; but that this integrity was native to man: so that in him by nature, as he was founded by God, and stood in this state, there were no inordinate motions: just as we say that some knowledge of God is natural, insofar as nothing is so natural, as what so sits in nature, that without its, so to speak, abjuration it cannot be removed. This justice therefore shone in Adam as soon as he arose, and he experienced nothing tepugnans [so the print; read repugnans, repugnant] to this justice.
pass_b: Finally Abraham Rambour, in the Syntagma of Sedan Theses, disputation on the image of God in man and original righteousness, thesis 27, gives his view on the question in these words: "We hold that original righteousness includes the whole integrity and holiness of man, and that it was natural to him. Loving God and obeying him were planted in Adam's nature from the moment it existed, and man excelled in this gift from the moment he was made.

"We do not want this to be taken as though this holiness flowed from the powers of nature, but in the sense that this integrity was native to man, so that in him, by nature as God made him and while he stood in that state, there were no disordered movements. In the same way we call some knowledge of God natural, since nothing is so natural as what is so lodged in nature that it cannot be removed without, so to speak, nature's renouncing it on oath. This righteousness, then, shone in Adam as soon as he came into being, and he felt nothing in himself that resisted it."

choices.why: The print reads 'tepugnans', a misprint for 'repugnans'; Pass B follows 'repugnans'.

notes: The 1675 print reads 'huic justitiae tepugnans'; this is a misprint for 'repugnans' ('resisting'), which the translation follows. Abraham Rambour taught theology at Sedan.

sections.title: Some Reformed make it natural as owed to nature's order; others, like Pareus, only as concreated and not superadded
sections.pass_a: But from these things it appears that many of the Reformed manifestly teach that Original justice was natural to the first man, since it was a perfection of the natural order, owed to a rational creature not yet corrupted by sin, as that which shines forth as it were from the faculties of human nature, which is supposed still pure and innocent: not otherwise than health and good condition from a body rightly disposed according to nature. But that others, as Pareus first of all, seem to call that justice natural to the first man only on this ground, that it was a certain perfection concreated with the first man, and which pertained to his native and Original endowments. And when they deny that it was supernatural, they mean nothing else than that it was not something superadded to the primeval and native endowments of man.
pass_b: From this it is plain that many of the Reformed openly teach that original righteousness was natural to the first man because it was a perfection of the natural order, owed to a rational creature not yet corrupted by sin, shining out, as it were, from the faculties of human nature, still taken to be pure and innocent, just as health and soundness shine out from a body that is in the condition nature intends.

Others, Pareus above all, seem to call that righteousness natural to the first man only because it was a perfection created together with him and belonged to his native, original endowments. When they deny it was supernatural, they mean only that it was not something added on top of man's first, native endowments.

choices.why: The first group's 'owed to nature' is the point Rome denies; the English keeps 'owed'.

sections.title: Common Reformed view: God's goodness forbids creating man without original righteousness, prone to evil
sections.pass_a: However that may be, and in whatever way finally Original justice is said to have been natural to the first man, the common opinion of the Reformed seems to be that it wholly conflicts with divine goodness and wisdom that God should found man without Original justice, and such a one as does not acknowledge and love God, as is right, and is prone and inclined to evil, and in whom sense and appetite fight against reason, and are rebels to the divine law. For they do not think that such privation of love toward God, and headlong inclination to evil and vices, and rebellion of sense and appetite against the mind, and the divine law, can in a rational creature lack sin and fault. And so they hold it absurd and injurious to the creator, if it is said that such rebellion of the lower faculties of the soul, and the proneness of the whole man to evil which follows from it, and repugnance to good, is something consequent on man's composition from rational soul and organic body, and which necessarily, and according to the very nature of things, results thence, unless God adds something above nature, which subjects reason to God, and subordinates the lower part of the soul to reason.
pass_b: However that may be, and on whatever ground original righteousness is said to have been natural to the first man, the common Reformed view seems to be that it is wholly at odds with God's goodness and wisdom for him to make man without original righteousness: a man who does not know and love God as he should, who leans and inclines toward evil, and in whom sense and appetite resist reason and rebel against God's law.

They do not believe that in a rational creature such a lack of love for God, such a headlong bent to evil and vice, and such a rebellion of sense and appetite against the mind and God's law, can be free of sin and guilt.

So they think it absurd, and an insult to the Creator, to say that this rebellion of the soul's lower faculties, with the proneness of the whole man to evil and his resistance to good that follow from it, is a consequence of man's being made of a rational soul and an organic body, something that results from that make-up necessarily and by the very nature of things unless God adds something above nature to subject reason to God and the lower part of the soul to reason.

choices.why: Culpa is moral guilt, not mere defect; the English says 'guilt'.

sections.title: So the Reformed think Rome's state of pure nature fictitious and impossible
sections.pass_a: And therefore they judge plainly fictitious and impossible that state of man in pure naturals, of which mention is often made in the Roman School; in which man is supposed not corrupted by sin, and yet empty of justice and sanctity, and not adhering to God with pure and chaste love, but drawn by his own concupiscence to lower things, ignorant of what things are necessary for true blessedness, weak and powerless to accomplish good, and inclined with headlong inclination to vices, as may be gathered from the dissertations of the Reformed Doctors who have been cited above, and of very many others, when they dispute about Original justice against Bellarmine, and other Doctors of the Roman School.
pass_b: They therefore regard as plainly fictitious and impossible the state of man "in a purely natural condition" that the Roman school so often speaks of. In it man is supposed to be uncorrupted by sin and yet empty of righteousness and holiness: not clinging to God with a pure and chaste love but dragged toward lower things by his own concupiscence, ignorant of what true blessedness requires, weak and unable to do good, and inclined headlong toward vice.

This can be gathered from the treatises of the Reformed teachers cited above, and of many others, where they argue about original righteousness against Bellarmine and other teachers of the Roman school.

choices.why: The quotation marks show this is Rome's technical phrase, which the Reformed reject.

sections.title: Pareus will not deny God could create man without original righteousness, only that he could make man whole without wholeness
sections.pass_a: Pareus however does not dare to assert that human nature could not have been created without Original justice. Nor do we say, he says, that human nature could not have been created by God without Original justice. For shall we set a limit to divine power? at least we say that God, when he founded integral man, could not deny himself; found integral man without integrity. In book 1. of Bellarm. on the Grace of the First man chap. 6. In the Response to the fourth reason.
pass_b: Pareus, however, does not venture to assert that human nature could not have been created without original righteousness. "We do not say," he writes, "that God could not have created human nature without original righteousness. Are we to put a boundary to God's power? What we do say is that when God made man whole, he could not deny himself by making a whole man without wholeness." (On Bellarmine, On the Grace of the First Man, book 1, chapter 6, reply to the fourth argument.)

choices.why: Pareus' wordplay on integer/integritas is kept with 'whole/wholeness'.

notes: 'He cannot deny himself' echoes 2 Timothy 2:13; the print gives no reference.

sections.title: Many Reformed still grant Adam supernatural gifts; du Moulin: revealed knowledge and constant help were supernatural
sections.pass_a: Further although the Reformed Doctors maintain that Original justice was natural to the first man, they will not however affirm, at least many of them, that the first man lacked all supernatural grace, and was adorned by God with no other than natural gifts. That is especially to be seen in Pierre du Moulin, in the disputation on the state of innocence cited above, thesis 49. and 50. We do not however deny, he says, that there were in Adam some supernatural gifts. For if he had drawn some knowledge from revelation: or if he had anything to which human nature however pure could not attain without a peculiar and extraordinary gift of God, that without doubt was supernatural: nor would Adam persisting in integrity have propagated it to posterity. Moreover just as there is no doubt that man however perfect his natural temperament of body, needs supernatural aid, and God's continual help, to preserve this eukrasia: so although Adam's nature was pure and holy, it yet needed constant supernatural aid to conserve that purity. Since even inanimate and irrational things are sustentur [so the print; read sustententur, sustained] by divine influx.
pass_b: Although the Reformed teachers maintain that original righteousness was natural to the first man, many of them at least will not say that he lacked all supernatural grace and that God adorned him with natural gifts only. This is especially clear in Pierre du Moulin, in the disputation on the state of innocence cited above, theses 49 and 50.

"We do not deny," he says, "that there were some supernatural gifts in Adam. If he drew any knowledge from revelation, or had anything that human nature, however pure, could not reach without a special and extraordinary gift of God, that was without doubt supernatural, and Adam would not have passed it on to his descendants even had he persevered in his integrity.

"Again, there is no doubt that a man, however perfect his body's natural balance, needs supernatural help and God's constant aid to keep that good balance (eukrasia). In the same way, though Adam's nature was pure and holy, it still needed continual supernatural help to keep that purity, since even lifeless and irrational things are upheld by God's inflowing power."

choices.why: The print has 'sustentur', a shortened or misprinted form of 'sustententur'; the sense 'are sustained' is certain.

notes: The 1675 print reads 'sustentur'; the translation takes it as 'sustententur' ('are sustained'). The eukrasia passage is the one Le Blanc cites in De Primi Hominis Immortalitate XXXV.

sections.title: Rambour: grace raised Adam's natural gifts, making him a son and heir, not only a faithful servant
sections.pass_a: Rambour similarly acknowledges in Adam supernatural gifts, in thesis twenty-nine of the disputation just cited. Nor on that account, he says, do we remove supernatural gifts from Adam. For the grace of God adorned these same natural gifts, raised them daily: just as grace does not destroy nature, but directs it, and raises it higher than it can strive by its own powers. Therefore the first man was not only an excellent creature, but also a son of God, taken up to receive the heavenly inheritance, that is, he had not only by nature the condition of a faithful servant, understanding well the will of the Lord, and carrying it out perfectly, but also by grace the dignity of a son hoping for the paternal blessing and inheritance.
pass_b: Rambour likewise recognizes supernatural gifts in Adam, in thesis 29 of the disputation just cited: "This does not mean that we take supernatural gifts away from Adam. God's grace adorned these same natural gifts and lifted them higher day by day, just as grace does not destroy nature but directs it and raises it higher than it can climb by its own strength.

"So the first man was not only an outstanding creature but also a son of God, adopted to enter into the heavenly inheritance. By nature he had the standing of a faithful servant who understood his Lord's will well and carried it out perfectly; by grace he also had the dignity of a son who hoped for his Father's blessing and inheritance."

choices.why: Cernere hereditatem is the Roman legal formula for formally accepting an inheritance.

notes: Adam as 'son of God' recalls Luke 3:38, and the servant-son contrast Galatians 4:7; the print gives no references.

sections.title: Tilenus: Rome slanders us as Pelagians; Adam's will was naturally upright but moved to act by grace, like a vine needing sun and rain
sections.pass_a: Things similar to which may be read in Tilenus. Criminally, he says, and calumniously the Papists fasten on us the opinion of the Pelagians, as if we contended that there were no supernatural gifts in the first man, when we attribute the Theological virtues to him expressly. On Original justice thesis thirty-eight. But a little before, explaining more distinctly in what the grace conferred on Adam consisted, As Adam's will had this from nature, he says, that it could work justly and holily, so that it should actually work, and love God above all, it was efficaciously moved by grace. But as a vine does not on that account lack natural force for producing wine, that it needs external aids, for instance sun, rain and cultivation, in order to produce in act, so also in Adam the rectitude of the will, and eutaxia of the affections, was not on that account not natural, although in second act it was exercised and helped by the aid of moving grace.
pass_b: Similar things can be read in Tilenus: "The papists wickedly and slanderously pin the Pelagians' view on us, as though we held there were no supernatural gifts in the first man, when we expressly ascribe the theological virtues to him." (On Original Righteousness, thesis 38.)

A little earlier, explaining more precisely what the grace given to Adam consisted in, he says: "Adam's will had from nature the power to act righteously and holily; that it actually did so, and loved God above all things, came from its being moved effectively by grace.

"But a vine is not without a natural power to bear wine just because it needs outside help, such as sun, rain and tending, to bear it in fact. In the same way the uprightness of Adam's will and the good order (eutaxia) of his affections were still natural, even though in their actual exercise they were set to work and helped by moving grace."

choices.why: Le Blanc's period term for adherents of the papacy, used by Tilenus in polemic; kept as historical usage.

notes: 'Second act' is the scholastic term for a power in actual operation, as distinct from the power itself (first act).

sections.title: Le Blanc: hard to see how faith, hope and love were supernatural yet righteousness natural; Rambour's statements do not fit together
sections.pass_a: Therefore that Doctor refers to supernatural grace in the first man both the actual aid by which he was stirred to act well, and the Theological virtues faith, hope, and charity with which he was adorned. But it can hardly be grasped how those virtues in Adam were supernatural gifts, and yet rectitude, or Original justice was natural to him, or what justice and Rectitude pleasing and accepted to God can be without faith, hope, and charity. As also in those things which we reported before from Rambour, the things which that most learned man affirms together do not seem to agree sufficiently among themselves, namely that the justice and sanctity of the first man was natural not supernatural, and yet that it did not flow from the powers of nature. For how can that not be supernatural which does not flow from the powers of nature? Unless we say that he with Pareus calls supernatural what is adventitious, and is superadded to native endowments. But that Original justice is called natural only on this ground, that it was implanted in man from the first Origin, and concreated with him, and so pertained to his native endowments; as he himself seems to explain himself. Although what he subjoins does not fit well, that the justice of the first man was natural to him, as some knowledge of God is natural to us. For that knowledge of God which he calls natural does not surpass the powers of nature.
pass_b: So Tilenus counts as supernatural grace in the first man both the actual help by which he was stirred to do good and the theological virtues, faith, hope and love, with which he was adorned. But it is hard to see how those virtues could have been supernatural gifts in Adam while his uprightness, or original righteousness, was natural to him. Or what righteousness and uprightness could please God and be accepted by him without faith, hope and love?

In the same way, in what we quoted earlier from Rambour, the things that very learned man asserts together do not seem to fit well: that the first man's righteousness and holiness was natural and not supernatural, and yet that it did not flow from the powers of nature. How can something not be supernatural if it does not flow from nature's powers?

Unless, that is, we say that he, like Pareus, calls supernatural whatever is acquired and added on top of native endowments, and calls original righteousness natural only because it was planted in man from his first origin, created together with him, and so belonged to his native endowments. That seems to be how he explains himself. Even so, what he adds does not quite square: that the first man's righteousness was natural to him as some knowledge of God is natural to us. The knowledge of God he calls natural does not go beyond nature's powers.

choices.why: The 'Doctor' is Tilenus, quoted in the previous thesis; the English names him.

notes: Faith, hope and love are the triad of 1 Corinthians 13:13; the print gives no reference.

sections.title: Summary: both schools agree the first man had true righteousness and holiness, with nothing disordered
sections.pass_a: But from those things which have been set out so far, it is plain that the Roman School, and the Reformed School agree in this, that the first man before the fall was endowed with true justice and sanctity, through which he both acknowledged God with the mind as is fitting, and loved him with the will, and had nothing in himself disordered, and which conflicted with the divine law and will, and which did not of its own accord submit itself to right reason.
pass_b: From what has been set out so far it is clear that the Roman and Reformed schools agree on this: before the fall the first man had true righteousness and holiness. Through it he knew God with his mind as he ought and loved him with his will, and he had nothing disordered in him, nothing at odds with God's law and will, nothing that would not freely submit to right reason.

choices.why: Le Blanc's summarizing formula; a plain English equivalent.

sections.title: Most Roman theologians agree with the Reformed that Adam was created in that righteousness
sections.pass_a: Thence also it is manifest that the Theologians of the Roman School, at least most of them, teach with the Reformed that the first man was created in that justice and sanctity; and so that the first man never lacked it, but that it was implanted in him from the first Origin.
pass_b: It is also clear from this that most theologians of the Roman school, at least, teach with the Reformed that the first man was created in that righteousness and holiness. He was therefore never without it; it was planted in him from his first origin.

choices.why: Origo is the moment of creation; 'origin' keeps the link with 'original righteousness'.
rejected: from the beginning of the world

sections.title: Hence most Roman doctors grant it was natural in the sense of native, not acquired
sections.pass_a: And therefore what manifestly follows thence, most Doctors of the Roman Church acknowledge with the Protestants that Original justice was natural to the first man, insofar as natural signifies the same as native, and is opposed to that which is adventitious and superadded.
pass_b: It plainly follows that most teachers of the Roman Church grant, with the Protestants, that original righteousness was natural to the first man in the sense in which "natural" means the same as "native" and is opposed to what is acquired and added on top.

choices.why: Le Blanc equates the two terms; quotation marks show they are words being compared.

sections.title: Some in Rome even hold, with most Reformed, that it was natural as opposed to supernatural
sections.pass_a: Indeed it is clear from those things which we reported before, that in the Roman Church there are not lacking those who with most of the Reformed teach that Original justice pertained to the gifts of nature, not of grace, as it is opposed to nature: and so that it was natural to the first man, insofar as natural is opposed to supernatural.
pass_b: In fact, what we reported earlier shows that the Roman Church has its own teachers who side with most of the Reformed here. They hold that original righteousness was one of nature's gifts, not one of grace's, taking grace as the opposite of nature. On their view it was natural to the first man even in the sense that stands against "supernatural".

lemmas.gloss: as grace is opposed to nature

choices.english: as grace is opposed to nature
choices.why: The implied subject is gratia; the English supplies it.

notes: Le Blanc means Medina's 'certain doctors' and those condemned with Baius (theses IV-V).

sections.title: Many in Rome grant the Reformed that God could not create man without it, so pure nature is a fiction
sections.pass_a: Moreover, as may be gathered from what has been said, in the Roman Church not a few grant to the Reformed that Original justice, of whatever kind it is finally to be called, whether natural, or supernatural, was a perfection so owed to innocent man, that saving divine wisdom and goodness, he could not be created without it: and so that the state of man in pure naturals, such as the common run of the Roman School describes, and in which man is supposed not a sinner, and yet empty of justice, and prone to vices, and laboring with concupiscence fighting against right reason, is something merely fictitious; and which divine goodness, justice, and wisdom forbid ever to be given in the nature of things.
pass_b: Again, as can be gathered from what has been said, a good many in the Roman Church grant the Reformed that original righteousness, whatever it should finally be called, natural or supernatural, was a perfection so owed to innocent man that God could not have created him without it without compromising his wisdom and goodness.

They grant too that the state of man in a purely natural condition, as the ordinary run of the Roman school describes it, in which man is supposed to be no sinner and yet empty of righteousness, prone to vice and struggling with a concupiscence that fights right reason, is a mere fiction, something God's goodness, justice and wisdom forbid ever to exist in reality.

lemmas.gloss: without compromising God's wisdom and goodness

choices.why: The scholastic phrase for actual existence; 'in reality' is the plain sense.
rejected: in the nature of things physically

notes: The Jansenists of theses XII-XVI are the chief Roman examples.

sections.title: The Protestants in turn grant it was not natural as constituting nature; many allow supernatural gifts and needed grace
sections.pass_a: But in turn the Protestants grant to the Doctors of the Roman School that Original justice was not natural to the first man, insofar as natural signifies that which constitutes nature, or what necessarily, or in a physical way, flows from the principles of human nature. And moreover many Doctors of the Reformed School do not deny that the first man had certain supernatural gifts: and that a certain grace was necessary to man, even innocent, so that he might work rightly and according to justice. Nay some of them confess that Original justice did not flow from the powers of nature.
pass_b: The Protestants, for their part, grant the teachers of the Roman school that original righteousness was not natural to the first man in the sense of what makes up nature, or of what flows necessarily, that is physically, from the principles of human nature.

Many teachers of the Reformed school also do not deny that the first man had some supernatural gifts, and that even innocent man needed some grace in order to act rightly and righteously. Some of them even admit that original righteousness did not flow from the powers of nature.

choices.why: Fateri is a concession; 'admit' keeps the concessive tone.

sections.title: The real controversy: natural or supernatural; real for some Reformed, verbal for others
sections.pass_a: But here there is a controversy between the Roman School, with very few excepted, and the Reformed School, Whether Original justice was natural to the first man, or supernatural. That it was natural not supernatural the Doctors of the Reformed School affirm by common consent; but on the contrary almost all the Theologians of the Roman School maintain that it was not natural, but supernatural. Which controversy indeed seems to be real in respect of some Theologians, but verbal in respect of others. It is real in respect of those who think that Original justice was a perfection of the natural order, answering to the natural faculties of man, and which pertained not to grace but to nature. For in reality the Theologians of the Roman School mean to signify the contrary, when they assert that that justice was supernatural. But the same controversy is verbal in respect of others, who teach that that justice was natural to the first man in no other way, than because it was concreated with him, and ought to be numbered among his native endowments. And when they deny that the same justice was supernatural, they mean to signify nothing else, than that it was not superadded to man above his primeval endowments. Which the Doctors of the Roman Church grant, at least very many of them.
pass_b: The real dispute here, between the Roman school (with very few exceptions) and the Reformed school, is whether original righteousness was natural or supernatural to the first man. The Reformed teachers say by common consent that it was natural and not supernatural; almost all the Roman theologians, on the other hand, insist that it was supernatural and not natural.

With some theologians this dispute seems to be about substance, with others only about words. It is a dispute of substance with those who hold that original righteousness was a perfection of the natural order, answering to man's natural faculties and belonging to nature rather than to grace. When the Roman theologians call that righteousness supernatural, they really do mean the opposite.

With the others it is a dispute about words. They teach that original righteousness was natural to the first man only because it was created with him and should be counted among his native endowments, and when they deny that it was supernatural they mean only that it was not added to man over and above his first endowments. That the Roman teachers grant, or a great many of them do.

choices.why: Reapse stresses an actual, not merely verbal, contrary meaning.

sections.title: A further question: does God's wisdom forbid creating man without it, and is 'pure nature' a possible state?
sections.pass_a: But moreover there is a question between the Reformed School and very many Doctors of the Roman School, Whether it does not conflict with divine wisdom and goodness that man be created without Original justice; and whether among the possible states of man that state ought to be numbered which the Roman School calls of pure nature: In which man is not corrupted by sin, and yet lacks true justice, and labors with much ignorance and infirmity, and is drawn to evil by his own concupiscence, and appetite rebelling against reason, not otherwise than the matter stands in the state of corrupt nature. Which the common run of the Doctors of the Roman Church affirms, but the Reformed School by common consent denies, with one perhaps or another excepted.
pass_b: There is a further question between the Reformed school and a great many Roman teachers: whether it is not contrary to God's wisdom and goodness for man to be created without original righteousness, and whether the state the Roman school calls "pure nature" should be counted among man's possible states.
