In that state man would not be corrupted by sin, yet would lack true righteousness, would struggle with much ignorance and weakness, and would be drawn toward evil by his own concupiscence and by an appetite rebelling against reason, just as things are in the state of corrupt nature. The ordinary run of Roman teachers says yes; the Reformed school, with perhaps one or two exceptions, says no by common consent.

lemmas.gloss: with perhaps one or two exceptions

choices.why: Quoted as Rome's technical term for the hypothetical state.

sections.title: First absurdity: God would be the author of concupiscence, which John says is not of the Father; Bellarmine's rust analogy fails
sections.pass_a: And certainly unless we so hold, most grave absurdities follow. For first it will follow thence that that concupiscence, through which the flesh fights against the spirit, and which the Doctors of the Roman School, even after Original sin is remitted, grant to have the character of vice, and of a certain moral evil, which is displeasing and hateful to God, and which John denies to be from the Father, it will follow, I say, thence that that concupiscence could have God himself as author; who namely, on this hypothesis, could have created man with it. Nor does what Bellarmine Responds take away the force of the argument, that that concupiscence would have emerged from matter, beyond God's intention: As rust from a sword, of which therefore the blacksmith is not the author. For the blacksmith did not make the matter of the iron whence rust arises, as God created the matter of our body. And yet, without the smith's fault, rust cannot be in a sword coming forth from his hands.
pass_b: Indeed, unless we hold this, the gravest absurdities follow. First, it will follow that God himself could be the author of the concupiscence by which the flesh fights against the spirit, since on this hypothesis he could have created man with it. Yet the Roman teachers grant that this concupiscence, even after original sin has been forgiven, has the character of a vice and of a moral evil that God finds displeasing and hateful, and John denies that it comes from the Father.

Bellarmine's reply does not remove the force of this argument. He says that concupiscence would have arisen from matter apart from God's intention, as rust arises on a sword, and the smith is not therefore its author. But the smith did not make the iron from which the rust comes, whereas God did create the matter of our bodies. And even so, rust cannot be on a sword fresh from the smith's hands unless the smith is at fault.

choices.english: unless the smith is at fault
choices.why: Citra = 'without, apart from'; recast positively for clarity.

notes: The flesh fighting the spirit is Galatians 5:17; John's denial that the lust of the flesh is 'of the Father' is 1 John 2:16. The print gives no references. Bellarmine's rust analogy is in De gratia primi hominis, chapter 5.

sections.title: Otherwise God would be the author of sin, or a rational creature could commit every crime without guilt
sections.pass_a: For supposing that God creates some man with the same ignorance, proneness to evil, and repugnance to good, with which we are now born from Adam; nor wills to help him with any supernatural grace, which the Scholastics commonly think can happen, that man will neither love God, nor compose his acts and affections to the norm of right reason, but will indulge his lust in all things, and will necessarily rush into diverse crimes, as occasion shall give itself; as a man born from Adam would do, if he were destitute of all aid of divine grace. And therefore so God will be the author of sin; as one who has created a man who by no fault of his own, but such as it seemed good to God to form him, cannot avoid sin, and by a certain vice and impulse of nature goes headlong into various crimes, nor is able to love his creator, as is right. Or it must be said that there can be given a rational creature, which will not be bound to acknowledge and love God, and which will be able to pollute itself with all uncleanness, and indulge wrath, luxury and gluttony, and rage against its likes with debaucheries and murders, and commit [so the print; read patrare, commit] the rest which the natural and eternal law forbids, and yet will not on that account become guilty of any crime and sin. Each of which is vehemently absurd; and involves a certain manifest impiety.
pass_b: Suppose God created a man with the same ignorance, the same leaning toward evil and resistance to good with which we are now born of Adam, and chose not to help him with any supernatural grace, as the scholastics commonly think could happen. That man would not love God or shape his acts and affections by the rule of right reason. He would give way to his desires in everything and would inevitably plunge into one crime after another as occasion arose, just as a child of Adam would do if he were left without any help from God's grace.

God would then be the author of sin, since he would have created a man who, through no fault of his own but simply because God chose to make him so, cannot avoid sin, rushes headlong into crimes of every kind by a flaw and drive in his nature, and cannot love his Creator as he ought.

Otherwise we would have to say there could be a rational creature not bound to know and love God, one that could defile itself with every impurity, give way to anger, excess and gluttony, assault its fellows with rape and murder, and do everything else the natural and eternal law forbids, and still not be guilty of any crime or sin. Both conclusions are utterly absurd and plainly involve impiety.

choices.why: The print has the passive form 'patrari' where the active 'patrare' is needed; the sense 'commit, do' is certain.

notes: The 1675 print reads 'patrari' (passive) where the construction needs 'patrare'; the translation follows the active sense.

sections.title: Granting that, whether original righteousness is called natural or supernatural matters less, if it is God's free gift
sections.pass_a: But this being once granted, that it cannot happen that man be created by God without justice and sanctity, that other question does not seem of so great moment. Whether that Justice and Sanctity in which God founded the first man, and without which he could not be created by God, pertains to the endowments of nature, or of grace, and is to be called natural, or supernatural: Provided, what all grant, we hold that it is a gratuitous gift of God, which was owed to no merits of the creature.
pass_b: Once it is granted that God cannot create man without righteousness and holiness, the other question does not seem so important: whether the righteousness and holiness in which God made the first man, and without which God could not have created him, belongs to the endowments of nature or of grace, and should be called natural or supernatural. That holds provided we affirm, as everyone grants, that it is God's free gift, owed to no merit of the creature.

choices.why: Modo with the subjunctive is a proviso; Le Blanc's irenic point depends on it.

sections.title: Yet reason favors calling it natural: what belongs to nature's right constitution and health is natural
sections.pass_a: Reason however seems to require that we say that it pertained to the endowments of nature, and was natural rather than supernatural. For that is natural not supernatural which pertains to the right constitution of nature, and without which nature is neither sound, nor rightly constituted. But now human nature without that Sanctity and Justice, which was in integral man, is not sound, but sick, nor can it be said rightly constituted; if indeed the rebellion of the lower faculties against reason, and the proneness of the whole man to rebelling against God, is a disease of rational nature and a certain vice.
pass_b: Still, reason seems to require us to say that it belonged to the endowments of nature and was natural rather than supernatural. What belongs to the right constitution of a nature, without which that nature is neither healthy nor rightly formed, is natural, not supernatural.

Human nature without the holiness and righteousness that unfallen man had is not healthy but sick, and cannot be called rightly formed, if indeed the rebellion of the lower faculties against reason and the whole man's tendency to rebel against God are a disease and a defect of rational nature.

choices.why: Le Blanc now gives his own view, cautiously ('seems').

sections.title: Second reason: what a rational creature needs to reach its natural end, knowing and loving God, is natural
sections.pass_a: Moreover to a rational creature not corrupted that is natural without which it cannot attain its natural end. But the end of a rational creature is that it acknowledge, love and worship God. For to this it was founded by God. But it cannot attain this end, if it be created without justice and sanctity; And if it be considered as destitute of those gifts which we lost through Adam's sin.
pass_b: Further, what an uncorrupted rational creature needs in order to reach its natural end is natural to it. The end of a rational creature is to know, love and worship God, for that is what God made it for.
It cannot reach that end if it is created without righteousness and holiness, that is, if it is thought of as stripped of the gifts we lost through Adam's sin.

choices.english: that is, if it is thought of
choices.why: The printed sentence 'Et si consideretur ...' is a fragment continuing the condition; the English joins it to the preceding clause as an explanation.
rejected: And even if it is considered

notes: The final printed sentence, 'Et si consideretur ut destituta donis illis quae per Adami peccatum amisimus', is a fragment; the translation reads it as restating the preceding condition.

sections.title: Third reason: every natural faculty has its natural perfection, and for the moral faculties that is righteousness
sections.pass_a: Nor also is there any natural faculty to which its natural perfection does not correspond. But the moral faculties, by reason of which man is capable of virtue and vice, are natural to man, no less than the others. But in what can their natural perfection consist, except in that very justice and sanctity, about which the question now is?
pass_b: Again, there is no natural faculty without a natural perfection that belongs to it. Man's moral faculties, which make him capable of virtue and vice, are as natural to him as his other faculties. What can their natural perfection be, if not the very righteousness and holiness now in question?

choices.why: Kept literal; the pair defines the moral faculties.

sections.title: Fourth reason: conformity to the law of nature belongs to pure nature, so the righteousness that makes it possible is natural
sections.pass_a: Add that it pertains to the endowments of nature in a rational creature not corrupt but pure, that it be conformable to the law of nature, and compose itself to its rules. And therefore whatever without which it cannot conform itself to the law of nature, and subject all its motions to it, does not exceed the endowments and order of nature. But man destitute of all justice and sanctity, and subject to those infirmities with which we are born today, cannot compose himself to the law of nature. And so that sanctity and justice, through which such infirmities are removed, must be judged to regard the gifts of nature not corrupt.
pass_b: Add that it belongs to the endowments of nature in a rational creature that is not corrupt but pure to conform to the law of nature and shape itself by its rules. So whatever it needs in order to conform to the law of nature and bring all its impulses under it does not go beyond the endowments and order of nature.

But a man without any righteousness or holiness, and subject to the weaknesses we are born with today, cannot shape himself by the law of nature. So the holiness and righteousness that remove such weaknesses must be counted among the gifts of uncorrupted nature.

lemmas.gloss: the endowments and order of nature

choices.english: whatever it needs in order to
choices.why: The printed 'quicquid sine quo' is elliptical ('whatever [is that] without which'); the English gives the sense.

sections.title: So it is inconsistent to say righteousness was natural yet Adam needed supernatural help to act; God's constant help can be of the natural order
sections.pass_a: Whence it seems also not to agree sufficiently with reason what some of the Reformed cited above say, that although that justice and sanctity in which the first man was created was natural to him, he yet needed a certain supernatural aid, by which he might be moved and stirred to act well. For although it is certain that without God's constant aid man never does anything good, not only in spiritual things, but not even in civil and human things: and so that before the fall itself man needed God's perpetual aid, in whom we live, move, and are: Yet it is not necessary that that aid was of the supernatural Order; but an aid could suffice for this which did not surpass the order of nature first instituted by God. For the aid required in order that every creature not yet corrupted and vitiated act conformably to its nature, and tend to its natural end, must be judged to pertain to the order of nature.
pass_b: So it also seems not quite reasonable for some of the Reformed cited above to say that, although the righteousness and holiness in which the first man was created were natural to him, he still needed a supernatural help to move and stir him to do good.

It is certain that without God's constant help man never does any good, not only in spiritual matters but not even in civil and human ones, so that even before the fall man needed the continual help of God, in whom we live and move and have our being. But that help did not have to be of the supernatural order. Help that did not go beyond the order of nature as God first established it could have been enough. The help a creature not yet corrupted and spoiled needs in order to act in keeping with its nature and tend toward its natural end should be reckoned as belonging to the order of nature.

choices.english: in whom we live and move and have our being
choices.why: Acts 17:28 in its familiar English form.

notes: Acts 17:28 is quoted without reference in the print. Le Blanc answers du Moulin and Tilenus (theses XXXVII and XXXIX).

sections.title: Still, God may have added supernatural gifts; Scripture is clear only that he revealed himself to Adam
sections.pass_a: But it does not follow thence that what many Reformed expressly teach is false, namely that there were in the first man certain supernatural gifts. For God could add to the endowments of primeval nature, and the aids necessary to it, what he pleased above nature; but what that was and how much, we do not dare, scripture being silent, to define. This however is certain from scripture, that there was in the first man a certain supernatural knowledge: since God revealed himself to him above nature, and taught him about his will by express word.
pass_b: It does not follow, however, that what many of the Reformed explicitly teach is false, namely that the first man had some supernatural gifts. God could have added to the endowments of man's first nature, and to the help it needed, whatever he pleased above nature. But what that was and how much, we do not venture to define, since Scripture is silent.
One thing Scripture does make certain: the first man had a certain supernatural knowledge, since God revealed himself to him beyond nature and taught him his will in express words.

choices.why: Le Blanc means spoken command, as in Genesis 2:16-17.

notes: God's express word to Adam is the command of Genesis 2:16-17; the print gives no reference.

sections.title: Body and soul do not make conflict natural: right order subjects the body's leanings to the soul
sections.pass_a: Nor from this, that man consists of an earthly body and a spiritual soul, does it follow that the fight of sense and appetite against reason is natural in him: and so that such fight and rebellion cannot be removed, except through a supernatural gift. For indeed a double inclination is natural to man, one toward earthly good, insofar as he is corporeal, but the other toward spiritual good, insofar as he is endowed with an intelligent soul: but just as the soul is far more excellent than its body, so also it befits nature rightly constituted, that the motions and inclinations of the body be subjected to the commands and orders of the soul, and thus appetite obey reason. But when the matter stands otherwise, in that appears a certain disordering of nature.
pass_b: It does not follow, from man's being made of an earthly body and a spiritual soul, that the conflict of sense and appetite with reason is natural in him, or that such conflict and rebellion can only be removed by a supernatural gift.

Man does naturally have two inclinations, one toward earthly good because he has a body, the other toward spiritual good because he has an intelligent soul. But as the soul far surpasses its body, so a rightly formed nature requires that the body's impulses and inclinations be subject to the soul's commands, and so that appetite obey reason. Where it is otherwise, nature is plainly out of order.

choices.why: Deordinatio is a rare scholastic word for disordering; the English uses a plain phrase.

notes: Le Blanc answers Bellarmine's two-propension argument (thesis IX).

sections.title: Nor is the fall hard to explain if rectitude was natural: the higher part turned from God, and disorder followed. De Justitia Primi Hominis closes
sections.pass_a: Nor, supposing that the rectitude concreated with man was itself natural, not supernatural, is it so difficult, as Bellarmine thinks, to show by what means that corruption which is now in us, and through which reason is forced to be subject to the affections, invaded human nature. For that vice had its origin from the higher part of the soul, when departing from God, it began to be borne toward the object of the sensitive appetite as toward its end. For thence followed the ataxia of the moral faculties in man. Since their primeval rectitude consisted in this, that all their motions and affections were directed to God as to the highest end, by the command of mind and reason. From which end reason cannot deviate, and substitute earthly goods for it, without being forced to serve basely, and against its own nature, sense and appetite, whose object is now in place of the highest end.
pass_b: Nor, granting that the rectitude created with man was itself natural and not supernatural, is it as hard as Bellarmine thinks to show how the corruption now in us, which forces reason to be subject to the passions, got into human nature.

That flaw began in the higher part of the soul, when it turned away from God and began to be carried toward the object of the sense appetite as though that were its end. The disorder (ataxia) of man's moral faculties followed from that. Their original rectitude lay in all their impulses and affections being directed, at the command of mind and reason, toward God as their highest end. Reason cannot turn aside from that end and put earthly goods in its place without being forced to serve sense and appetite, shamefully and against its own nature, since their object now stands for it in place of the highest end.

choices.why: Affectus here are the lower movements that reason should govern; 'passions' fits the faculty psychology.
